content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper introduces a new approach for selective classification based on disagreement of model checkpoints with the final model prediction. To this end, two scores are proposed to understand when the model should abstain from making decision. The superior score is calculated by weighted averaging over the disagreement values of the checkpoints where smaller weights are given to the later checkpoints. The authors believe that this is the first method for selective classification which can be applied to any existing model without any modification and by just storing some checkpoints during the training.

The authors list the following items as their contributions: Proposing a new algorithm based on disagreement of label predictions between the intermediate models and the final model. Finding an upper-bound on the probability of a test point being correctly classified. Experimental studies comparing the proposed model with other selective models on benchmark datasets, and showing it can provide comparable results with the SOTA model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
* The paper has lots of experimental studies and comparison with the state-of-the-art models
* The visualizations are insightful and interesting. Specially, I liked the ones in Figure 6, showing the patterns for optimized points overlaps with correctly classified test-time points.
* The theoretical analysis to find and upper-bound for the probability of a test point being correctly classified.

### Weakness
* In general, selective classification is intuitively tied to uncertainty estimation, and that's why SR and MC-Dropouts are the simple baselines. On the other hand, using ensemble models for uncertainty estimation is a very popular approach. Also, using checkpoints for ensembling is an old idea used in deep probabilistic models or some simple papers (e.g. Checkpoint Ensembles: https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.03282). The authors also cited some of those work at the end of Section 2. Maybe, the other ensemble models with uncertainty estimation could achieve similar results as what presented in this paper. Thus, my major concern is that this work is very incremental in terms of novelty and significant for publication in ICLR. 
* The model does not beat SAT. But, this is not my reason for making the decision.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* The paper is fairly clear
* The experiments and visualizations are thorough and complete
* I have concerns about novelty as I mentioned above.
* The work seems reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: As I mentioned above, the idea of using checkpoints as ensemble models and using ensembles for uncertainty estimation is popular in the literature. So, I feel this paper is lacking the required novelty and significant for publication in ICLR.

content.title: Response to Reviewer WQqU
content.comment:
Thank you for your feedback.

>_**In general, selective classification is intuitively tied to uncertainty estimation, and that's why SR and MC-Dropouts are the simple baselines. On the other hand, using ensemble models for uncertainty estimation is a very popular approach. Also, using checkpoints for ensembling is an old idea used in deep probabilistic models or some simple papers (e.g. Checkpoint Ensembles: https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.03282). The authors also cited some of those work at the end of Section 2. Maybe, the other ensemble models with uncertainty estimation could achieve similar results as what presented in this paper. Thus, my major concern is that this work is very incremental in terms of novelty and significant for publication in ICLR.**_

We would like to point out that we perform better than the usual ensembling approaches (see Table 1 where for some datasets we improve over MC-Dropout by over 15%). The core question this paper is addressing is not that one can obtain ensembles for cheap/from checkpoints, it is how should we ensemble? 

All past work on ensembling for selective classification (we are aware of, including  https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.03282) considers averaging the predictions (and/or computing second moments) to get a better estimator of a model’s prediction (and/or uncertainty). Instead we investigate using checkpoints/ensembles as a means to check if a datapoint follows temporal patterns typical of datapoints we (could have) trained on; that is, from a plausibility for the training run perspective. What we showed was that this approach to using ensembles leads to significantly better results for selective classification than a typical ensemble approach, and matches current SOTA selective classification (note these SOTA methods are not ensemble based). We wish to point out that we continue to match SOTA selective classification on ImageNet (see Table 7), and are the first to report results on ImageNet. One can interpret our results as saying “plausible (or optimized) = correct”, the hypothesis in our method, holds more often than “low uncertainty (or high confidence) = correct”, the hypothesis in typical ensembling. Hence, we believe this paper initiates a fruitful connection between work on the privacy/security of machine learning and selective classification (and uncertainty estimation in general).

To elaborate more on this connection, this selective classification result can be viewed as a consequence of a better understanding of the composition of the set of plausible datapoints. Plausible here means that there is a dataset including that datapoint which can reproduce a specific training trajectory leading to the final model. In other words, given a training trajectory, could it have come from using a particular datapoint? Understanding the plausible set has implications for various aspects of trustworthy machine learning, as discussed by Thudi et al. (cited in our submission) who proved the plausible set can be strictly larger than the original training dataset. In this paper we take the first steps in understanding the composition of the plausible set by empirically relating a weakened probabilistic notion of plausibility to the set of correct in-distribution datapoints (limiting ourselves to in-distribution data).

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a method for selective classification that is based on training dynamics. The main idea is to collect predictions on a datapoint from several checkpoints and using the agreement between these predictions, a datapoint is rejected or not. The paper presents a comparison between the proposed method and the other selective classification baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper is well-written and easy to follow
- The paper include several experiments on the proposed method

Weakness:
- The proposed method is overcomplicated and the empirical results do not justify the benefits. If we need to use 25/50 checkpoints to get good performance, this is too much computation. We have to store these checkpoints and run inference for each checkpoint to get a prediction. Why not train a deep ensemble model with 10 ensemble members and get 10 independent predictions from fully-trained models instead? If we want to do the training once, we can use the approach from Huang 2016 [A] where 6 snapshots were enough to get good performance.
- I understand that CIFAR-10 and Cats & Dogs were used in the original SelectiveNet paper and the SAT paper. However, these datasets are saturated. For 70% coverage, the error is close to 0. The paper should have tried a dataset such as ImageNet where the difference between the methods will be clearer. 
- It would have been interesting to extend the proposed method to regression and see the performance.

[A] Huang G, Li Y, Pleiss G, Liu Z, Hopcroft JE, Weinberger KQ. Snapshot ensembles: Train 1, get m for free. arXiv preprint arXiv:1704.00109. 2017 Apr 1. (ICLR 2017)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is clear.
Novelty: The proposed idea is novel for selective classification but it is similar to ideas such as snapshot ensembles. 
Reproducibility: It is not clear if the code will be released
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents an ensemble-like method to determine wether to make a prediction on a datapoint or abstain. The proposed method requires using several checkpoints to check for the agreement between the checkpoints and the model final prediction. Give the number of checkpoints required, the heuristics in deciding when to abstain, and the simplicity of the other baselines, I think the proposed method is not practical and will not be widely adopted.

content.title: Response to Reviewer gqL7
content.comment:
Thank you for your feedback.

>_**The proposed method is overcomplicated and the empirical results do not justify the benefits. If we need to use 25/50 checkpoints to get good performance, this is too much computation. We have to store these checkpoints and run inference for each checkpoint to get a prediction. Why not train a deep ensemble model with 10 ensemble members and get 10 independent predictions from fully-trained models instead? If we want to do the training once, we can use the approach from Huang 2016 [A] where 6 snapshots were enough to get good performance.**_

We would like to point out that we perform better than the usual ensembling approaches (see Table 1 where for some datasets we improve over MC-Dropout by over 15%). The core question this paper is addressing is not that one can obtain ensembles for cheap, it is _how should we ensemble_? 

All past work on ensembling for selective classification we are aware of, including Huang 2016, considers averaging the predictions (and/or computing second moments) to get a better estimator of a model’s prediction (and/or uncertainty). Instead we investigate using checkpoints/ensembles as a means to check if a datapoint follows _temporal_ patterns typical of datapoints we (could have) trained on; that is, from a plausibility for the training run perspective. What we showed was that this approach to using ensembles leads to significantly better results for selective classification than a typical ensemble approach, and matches current SOTA selective classification (note these SOTA methods are not ensemble based).  One can interpret this as saying “plausible (or optimized) = correct”, the hypothesis in our method, holds more often than “low uncertainty (or high confidence) = correct”, the hypothesis in typical ensembling. Hence, we believe this paper initiates a fruitful connection between work on the privacy/security of machine learning and selective classification (and uncertainty estimation in general).

To elaborate more on this connection, this selective classification result can be viewed as a consequence of a better understanding of the composition of the set of plausible datapoints. Plausible here means that there is a dataset including that datapoint which can reproduce a _specific training trajectory_ leading to the final model. In other words, given a training trajectory, could it have come from using a particular datapoint? Understanding the plausible set has implications for various aspects of trustworthy machine learning, as discussed by Thudi et al. (cited in our submission) who proved the plausible set can be strictly larger than the original training dataset. In this paper we take the first steps in understanding the composition of the plausible set by empirically relating a weakened probabilistic notion of plausibility to the set of correct in-distribution datapoints (limiting ourselves to in-distribution data).

>_**I understand that CIFAR-10 and Cats & Dogs were used in the original SelectiveNet paper and the SAT paper. However, these datasets are saturated. For 70% coverage, the error is close to 0. The paper should have tried a dataset such as ImageNet where the difference between the methods will be clearer.**_

We would like to refer the reviewer to Table 7 (in appendix) in which we provide results for ImageNet. We find that our method continues to match or outperform SOTA selective classification performance. We wish to point out that, to the best of our knowledge, no prior SC paper has previously reported results on an ImageNet like scale.

>_**It would have been interesting to extend the proposed method to regression and see the performance**_

It is indeed possible to adapt our selective classification technique to a more general selective prediction technique that can handle a regression application scenario. Instead of monitoring a discrete label prediction over time, we can monitor a real-valued prediction over time. Then, to measure the noisiness of this prediction sequence, we could monitor the weighted variance of this prediction as proposed in appendix B.3. We note that numerous previous selective prediction approaches designed for classification are instead not directly translatable into the regression setting (e.g. adding an additional rejection class).

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on the setting of selective classification, which allows the model to reject certain examples if not confident enough. It proposes to use training dynamics for selective classification. Training dynamics has been used before to characterize different types of training examples. It’s quite an interesting idea to leverage training dynamics for  selective classification.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
1. The idea of using training dynamics for selective classification is novel and interesting
2. Experimental results look promising.

Weaknesses
1. In the introduction, the authors motivate their method by saying “these modifications are unnecessary”, because existing selective classification techniques either modify the model architecture or loss function. I am not sure if this motivation is convincing enough. As long as the modification is reasonable and easy to adopt, I don’t see any problems with modifications. For example, Deep Gamblers from  Liu et al. (2019 ) modifies the loss function in a very simple way which can be implemented in 5 lines of PyTorch code (see Appendix 8.1 from Liu et al. (2019 )). 
2. On the other hand, the authors claim that the proposed methods can be applied to any models as long as intermediate checkpoints have been saved while they were trained. I am afraid that this requirement may not be as often satisfied as the authors have hoped. Firstly, too many checkpoints have huge storage costs, especially given the model size is becoming bigger and bigger. A common way to deal with it is via overwriting the previous checkpoint file whenever we want to generate a new one. For example, only the latest checkpoint file (or just a few checkpoint files) may be kept in storage in case of failure. It’s not clear at least how many checkpoints are needed for the proposed method to perform well. Secondly, I am not sure if we can apply the proposed method “retroactively” to a model already in deployment (as suggested by the authors in the Introduction). This is because we normally need just one checkpoint to deploy a model (typically the checkpoint with the best validation accuracy). Therefore, other checkpoints are very likely to have been purged (or only a few are kept) for storage purposes. 
3. In section 3.3, the authors assume the expected values for p_t is 0 for all t, i.e., e_t =0 for all t. This is only empirically true for easy datasets according to Figure 6. For hard datasets such as CIFAR100 as shown in Figure 6d, this assumption does not hold. I suppose the authors’ purpose is not to design a method just for easy datasets. Therefore, I am concerned with this assumption.
4. The Table 1 and 2 show the results for either a given target error or target coverage. It’s not clear how to choose the threshold $\tau$ for a given target error or target coverage.  
5. Table 1 and 2 only contain results for easy datasets such as CIFAR10, SVHN and CATS-Dogs. I am curious about the performance on hard datasets such as CIFAR100 or ImageNet, because the assumption (as I mentioned in the third point) is violated on these datasets. I am not sure if the proposed methods can still outperform the baselines on these datasets.
6. I am also concerned with the inference time cost for the proposed methods, because each testing example needs to go through all these checkpoints.
content.summary_of_the_review: The idea of using training dynamics is interesting, but I have som concerns regarding the motivation, assumption and datasets used in this paper.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Response to Reviewer RqEB
content.comment:
Thank you for your feedback.

>_**In the introduction, the authors motivate their method by saying “these modifications are unnecessary”, because existing selective classification techniques either modify the model architecture or loss function. I am not sure if this motivation is convincing enough. As long as the modification is reasonable and easy to adopt, I don’t see any problems with modifications. For example, Deep Gamblers from Liu et al. (2019 ) modifies the loss function in a very simple way which can be implemented in 5 lines of PyTorch code (see Appendix 8.1 from Liu et al. (2019 )).**_

We would like to point out that it is not known if such modifications can still consistently lead to SOTA performing models. More generally, there is limited literature on how one can use such modification in various training pipelines that impose constraints on the optimizer. The simple scientific merit of what we have shown is that you can obtain SOTA selective classification by simply inspecting any existing training run. 

>_**On the other hand, the authors claim that the proposed methods can be applied to any models as long as intermediate checkpoints have been saved while they were trained. I am afraid that this requirement may not be as often satisfied as the authors have hoped. Firstly, too many checkpoints have huge storage costs, especially given the model size is becoming bigger and bigger. A common way to deal with it is via overwriting the previous checkpoint file whenever we want to generate a new one. For example, only the latest checkpoint file (or just a few checkpoint files) may be kept in storage in case of failure. It’s not clear at least how many checkpoints are needed for the proposed method to perform well. Secondly, I am not sure if we can apply the proposed method “retroactively” to a model already in deployment (as suggested by the authors in the Introduction). This is because we normally need just one checkpoint to deploy a model (typically the checkpoint with the best validation accuracy). Therefore, other checkpoints are very likely to have been purged (or only a few are kept) for storage purposes.**_

On only keeping the last checkpoints, Table 6 (in the appendix) presents results on the effectiveness of our approach when only using the last fraction of checkpoints. We see one can get away with using significantly fewer checkpoints (that is, checkpoints from the last parts of training). On applying retroactively to all models, we will emphasize more the need for multiple checkpoints in the introduction (currently stated in the contribution bullet-point but missing in the other bolded sentences in the introduction).

>_**In section 3.3, the authors assume the expected values for p_t is 0 for all t, i.e., e_t =0 for all t. This is only empirically true for easy datasets according to Figure 6. For hard datasets such as CIFAR100 as shown in Figure 6d, this assumption does not hold. I suppose the authors’ purpose is not to design a method just for easy datasets. Therefore, I am concerned with this assumption.**_

In appendix C 3.3 (Figure 12) we included results for the performance of our method when also incorporating a more accurate estimate of $e_t$. What we see is no significant change in performance, and hence we kept the simpler methods in the main body. We would also like to mention that results for ImageNet (a “hard” dataset) are presented in Table 7 in the appendix, which shows we continue to match SOTA. We wish to point out that we are the first to report selective classification results on ImageNet.

>_**The Table 1 and 2 show the results for either a given target error or target coverage. It’s not clear how to choose the threshold τ for a given target error or target coverage.**_

As is consistent with past work in comparing different methods, we fix a desired coverage/error and pick the threshold that gives that error/coverage on the test set. By doing this we get an accurate comparison of what the best performance of each method is. In practice, one could not do this for their test set, which is why one might consider different approaches to tuning a threshold (using a validation set, actively adjusting, etc.). We believe studying optimal tuning mechanisms for selective classification thresholds is out of scope for the current paper.
